title: BCNF
description: Understand Boyce-Codd normal form through overlapping candidate keys, a lossless decomposition and a concrete dependency-preservation counterexample.

references.title: Database System Concepts relational database design

questions.question_text: What is the single defining difference between 3NF and BCNF?
options: BCNF requires 1NF but 3NF does not
3NF allows a non-superkey determinant if the attribute it determines is prime; BCNF requires every determinant to be a superkey with no exceptions
BCNF only applies to relations with a single attribute
3NF is stricter than BCNF
questions.explanation: This 'prime attribute' escape clause is precisely what 3NF relaxes and BCNF removes — BCNF has zero tolerance for non-superkey determinants.

questions.question_text: In SectionAssignment(StudentID, CourseID, InstructorID) with FDs {StudentID, CourseID}->InstructorID and InstructorID->CourseID, why does InstructorID->CourseID violate BCNF?
options: Because InstructorID is never functionally dependent on anything
Because InstructorID's closure alone does not reach StudentID, so InstructorID is not a superkey, yet it determines CourseID
Because CourseID cannot appear on the right-hand side of any FD
Because InstructorID and CourseID have the same data type
questions.explanation: BCNF requires every determinant to be a superkey. InstructorID alone only determines {InstructorID, CourseID}, missing StudentID, so it fails the superkey test outright.

questions.question_text: Why does the SAME functional dependency (InstructorID -> CourseID) NOT violate 3NF in this relation?
options: Because 3NF ignores functional dependencies entirely
Because CourseID is a prime attribute (it belongs to the candidate key {StudentID, CourseID}), satisfying 3NF's escape clause even though InstructorID is not a superkey
Because InstructorID happens to be a superkey after all
Because 3NF only checks composite determinants
questions.explanation: 3NF's condition (b) — the right-hand side consists only of prime attributes — is satisfied here since CourseID participates in a candidate key, letting this FD pass 3NF despite failing BCNF.

questions.question_text: What are the two candidate keys of SectionAssignment(StudentID, CourseID, InstructorID)?
options: {StudentID} and {CourseID} individually
{StudentID, CourseID} and {StudentID, InstructorID}
{CourseID} and {InstructorID} individually
{StudentID, CourseID, InstructorID} is the only candidate key
questions.explanation: Both pairs' closures reach all three attributes: {StudentID, CourseID} directly determines InstructorID, and {StudentID, InstructorID} reaches CourseID via InstructorID->CourseID — and neither can be reduced further.

questions.question_text: Which decomposition brings SectionAssignment into BCNF?
options: Merging it with the Enrollment table
InstructorCourse(InstructorID, CourseID) and StudentInstructor(StudentID, InstructorID), so InstructorID is a proper superkey in the first relation
Adding a fourth candidate key
Removing InstructorID from the relation entirely
questions.explanation: Splitting along the violating FD makes InstructorID a full key of its own relation (InstructorCourse), and the remaining relation's determinant is also a superkey — both now satisfy BCNF.

questions.question_text: Why is no further BCNF split needed for Student(StudentID, StudentName), Instructor(InstructorID, InstructorName, InstructorOffice), Course(CourseID, CourseName, InstructorID) and Enrollment(StudentID, CourseID, EnrollmentDate), assuming only their identifier/key dependencies?
options: Foreign keys make every relation BCNF automatically
Each relation’s nontrivial determinants are superkeys under those stated dependencies
BCNF applies only to three-column relations
None of the relations is in 3NF
questions.explanation: Check the stated projected dependencies. The conclusion follows from superkey determinants, not from names or a general absence-of-overlap shortcut.

questions.question_text: What is a known trade-off/caveat when decomposing a relation into BCNF?
options: BCNF decomposition always increases redundancy
BCNF decomposition can sometimes fail to preserve all original functional dependencies without needing an extra join to re-check them
BCNF decomposition is illegal in SQL
BCNF relations can never have foreign keys
questions.explanation: Unlike most 3NF decompositions, some BCNF decompositions lose the ability to check certain original FDs without joining tables back together — a recognized, if uncommon, trade-off.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the relationship between BCNF and 3NF is correct?
options: Every 3NF relation is automatically in BCNF
Every BCNF relation is automatically in 3NF, but not every 3NF relation is in BCNF
BCNF and 3NF are entirely unrelated conditions
A relation can be in BCNF without being in 1NF
questions.explanation: BCNF is strictly stronger than 3NF — satisfying BCNF's superkey-only rule automatically satisfies 3NF's looser rule, but the reverse doesn't hold, as the SectionAssignment example shows.

questions.question_text: For a nontrivial BCNF dependency X→Y, what must X be?
options: A superkey
Any prime attribute
A foreign key only
The shortest name
questions.explanation: BCNF requires the determinant to identify the full relation.

questions.question_text: Does prime mean an attribute alone is unique?
options: Yes, always
No, it means membership in some candidate key
Only for integer attributes
Only for generated identifiers
questions.explanation: A composite-key component can be prime without identifying rows alone.

questions.question_text: What proves this binary decomposition lossless?
options: Both table names are short
The shared InstructorID determines the InstructorCourse component
Every current sample has two rows
The join uses ORDER BY
questions.explanation: The common determinant is a key of one component under the original dependencies.

questions.question_text: Can losslessness and dependency preservation differ?
options: No, they are synonyms
Only without primary keys
Yes
Only with three tables
questions.explanation: They ask about reconstruction and local enforcement respectively.

questions.question_text: Two instructors map to one course and a student maps to both. Which original rule can fail?
options: InstructorID→CourseID necessarily
Every primary key necessarily
Every foreign key necessarily
StudentID, CourseID→InstructorID
questions.explanation: The reconstructed student-course pair can have two instructors while local keys hold.

questions.question_text: Must every BCNF design be preferable to every 3NF design?
options: No, enforcement and workload trade-offs matter
Yes, regardless of lost dependencies
Only if its names are alphabetical
Only with fewer tables
questions.explanation: A normalization decision must preserve the required behavior through an enforceable design.

questions.question_text: Does a primary key declaration alone prove BCNF?
options: Yes, by definition
No, other nontrivial dependencies may violate it
Only for text keys
Only when the table is empty
questions.explanation: All relevant domain dependencies must be inspected.

questions.question_text: After splitting a relation, which dependencies govern each component?
options: Every original rule with missing columns unchanged
Only the first listed rule
Its projected implied dependencies
Only dependencies named after the table
questions.explanation: Dependencies must be meaningful over the component’s own attributes.

questions.question_text: Can choosing different violating dependencies yield different decompositions?
options: No, only one arrangement is possible
Only when a password changes
Only if SQL is unavailable
Yes
questions.explanation: Each outcome needs its own lossless and preservation analysis.

questions.question_text: Does BCNF automatically remove every multivalued-dependency anomaly?
options: No
Yes, for all relations
Only when COUNT is used
Only for a numeric key
questions.explanation: Fourth normal form imposes additional conditions on multivalued dependencies.

questions.question_text: What does a counterexample query returning no rows establish?
options: The dependency for every future legal state
No observed conflict in that current sample
Every projected table is BCNF
All writes are authorized
questions.explanation: Sample validation is narrower than a domain-level proof.

questions.question_text: Why does the independently populated two-table example not refute losslessness?
options: It lacks an ORDER BY alias
Lossless means no constraints exist
It is not the projection of a legal original relation
The table names are different
questions.explanation: Losslessness reconstructs legal original states, not every arbitrary independent component state.

notes:
## Require every nontrivial determinant to identify the relation

A relation is in Boyce-Codd normal form, or BCNF, when every nontrivial functional dependency implied by its dependency set has a superkey as its determinant. For X→Y, trivial means Y is contained in X. A superkey determines every attribute of the relation. The rule applies to all implied dependencies, not just the handful a designer happens to list in a diagram.

BCNF targets redundancy caused by functional dependencies whose determinants do not identify the entire relation. It is stricter than third normal form. Third normal form permits a nontrivial dependency with a non-superkey determinant when the dependent attribute is prime, meaning it belongs to some candidate key. BCNF removes that exception. Neither definition can compensate for an incorrect dependency assumption or an incomplete account of the domain.

## Build an example with overlapping candidate keys

Consider SectionAssignment(StudentID, CourseID, InstructorID). Assume each student-course pair chooses one instructor, and each instructor teaches exactly one course in this designed setting. The dependencies are StudentID, CourseID→InstructorID and InstructorID→CourseID. These are explicit modeling assumptions; a real institution allowing one instructor to teach several courses would need a different dependency set and might reach a different normal-form conclusion.

The pair StudentID, CourseID determines all three attributes directly. The pair StudentID, InstructorID also determines all three because the instructor supplies CourseID. Neither pair has a removable attribute under these dependencies, so both are candidate keys. StudentID, CourseID and InstructorID are all prime attributes because each appears in at least one of those keys. Prime does not mean unique by itself.

InstructorID alone determines CourseID but not StudentID. It is therefore not a superkey for the whole relation. Its dependency to CourseID is nontrivial and violates BCNF. It does not violate the third-normal-form condition because CourseID is prime. This small example explains precisely why third normal form and BCNF differ without relying on a vague claim that one simply has fewer tables.

## See the redundancy in actual rows

Suppose learner seven studies databases with instructor ten and learner eight studies the same course with instructor ten. Both rows repeat that instructor ten teaches databases. Changing the course assignment requires coordinated updates to multiple rows. Deleting the final student-instructor assignment can also remove the only stored fact about which course that instructor teaches, even if that association should still exist independently.

```sql
CREATE TABLE section_assignment (
  student_id INT NOT NULL,
  course_id INT NOT NULL,
  instructor_id INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY(student_id,course_id),
  UNIQUE(student_id,instructor_id)
);
INSERT INTO section_assignment VALUES (7,4,10),(8,4,10);
```

The SQL declares two unique combinations, but those declarations alone do not enforce InstructorID→CourseID across different students. A third row for another student and the same instructor with a different course can still satisfy both declared combinations while violating the modeled dependency. Treat the SQL as an illustration of the redundancy, not proof that all assumed dependencies are already enforced.

## Decompose along the violating dependency

Split the relation into InstructorCourse(InstructorID, CourseID) and StudentInstructor(StudentID, InstructorID). In the first relation, InstructorID is a key and determines the course. In the second, the complete pair identifies the association; under the stated projected dependencies there is no nontrivial determinant violating BCNF. The instructor-course fact is stored once instead of repeated for each student.

The decomposition is lossless under the original dependencies. The common attribute InstructorID determines all attributes of InstructorCourse, satisfying the binary decomposition losslessness test. Projecting a legal original relation and joining those projections on InstructorID reconstructs the original tuples without inventing extra combinations. That conclusion depends on the stated dependency; an arbitrary split sharing an arbitrary column would not have the same guarantee.

```sql
SELECT si.student_id, ic.course_id, si.instructor_id
FROM student_instructor si
JOIN instructor_course ic ON ic.instructor_id=si.instructor_id
ORDER BY si.student_id, ic.course_id;
```

For the two-row example, the reconstructed result contains student seven/course four/instructor ten and student eight/course four/instructor ten. The join does not magically validate every future set of independent writes to the decomposed tables. Valid reconstruction of the current projections and preservation of all original constraints are different questions.

## Identify the dependency-preservation trade-off

After decomposition, a student could be associated with instructor ten and instructor eleven while both instructors map to the same course. Each individual table can satisfy its local keys, yet the join then gives one student-course pair with two instructors. This violates the original StudentID, CourseID→InstructorID dependency. The split is lossless for legal original states but does not preserve that dependency through local checks alone.

This distinction is central to design decisions. Losslessness asks whether projections of a legal original relation reconstruct it correctly. Dependency preservation asks whether enforcing the projected dependencies suffices to enforce the original set without joining relations. One property does not imply the other. A BCNF decomposition can require an additional trusted constraint mechanism, a reviewed transaction protocol or a reconsidered design to enforce a dependency spanning the split.

A dependency-preserving third-normal-form design can be preferable when its remaining redundancy is understood and its local enforcement fits the workload. BCNF is not an instruction to ignore constraint enforcement or optimize an acronym at any cost. Document the anomaly removed, the dependencies retained locally and any rules now requiring cross-table checks. Evaluate writes and failures as well as the convenience of a reporting join.

## Apply the definition beyond the worked example

For each candidate violating dependency, compute the determinant's closure over the relation under examination. If it covers all attributes, the determinant is a superkey and that dependency is not a BCNF violation. If it does not and the dependency is nontrivial, a decomposition candidate exists. After a split, recompute projected dependencies for each component rather than copying every original rule unchanged into every smaller relation.

A decomposition algorithm can produce different valid results depending on which violation is chosen first. Each result still needs a losslessness argument and an explicit preservation analysis. A collection of tables with primary keys does not automatically establish BCNF, because an undeclared domain dependency can remain inside one of them. Conversely, a relation can already satisfy BCNF and still require separate treatment of multivalued dependencies in fourth normal form.

## Avoid shortcuts based on names and current data

A column called id is not automatically the only candidate key, and a name column is not automatically a determinant. State which legal states the application permits. A sample with no repeated instructors may hide the redundancy completely, while a larger legal sample reveals it. An SQL query finding no current conflicting pairs is useful diagnostic evidence, but it does not prove the dependency for all future states.

The enrollment decomposition into Student, Instructor, Course and Enrollment can satisfy BCNF when each of its nontrivial determinants is a key under the actual projected dependencies. That conclusion follows from inspecting the dependencies, not merely from the tables having different names or from the absence of overlapping keys. Different requirements can add a new determinant and invalidate a previously sound conclusion.

## Check operations that introduce new associations

Test insertion as well as reconstruction. Adding an instructor-course row should not require inventing a student, and removing the final student assignment should not erase an instructor's course fact. Conversely, adding a student's second instructor must still respect the original per-course choice rule. These separate tests make the benefit and the unresolved enforcement cost of the split visible to the team maintaining the write paths.

## Solve two design exercises

First exercise: compute InstructorID+ in SectionAssignment and explain why its course dependency violates BCNF but passes third normal form. The solution is InstructorID and CourseID only; StudentID is missing, while CourseID is prime. Then show both candidate-key closures and remove one attribute from each to establish minimality rather than relying on the labels in the diagram.

Second exercise: populate InstructorCourse with instructors ten and eleven both teaching course four, and StudentInstructor with student seven assigned to both. The join reveals the lost student-course-to-instructor restriction. Explain why this does not refute the lossless decomposition theorem: the independently constructed state is not a projection of a legal original state. Continue with [attribute closure](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/closure-of-attributes), [third normal form](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/3nf) and [fourth normal form](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/4nf) to distinguish these guarantees.

diagrams.description: InstructorCourse stores one course per instructor. StudentInstructor stores pairs. Their local keys permit one student to choose two instructors of the same course, violating the original student-course rule.
